item.title: Two alleged robbers sought after Suva home invasion
item.description: Prakash shared a video on social media showing the extent of the damage and disarray inside the house, allegedly after two robbers broke into the property. In his message, Prakash said the incident had deeply affected his family, but thanked God that everyone was safe.
item.content:encoded:
Prakash shared a video on social media showing the extent of the damage and disarray inside the house, allegedly after two robbers broke into the property.

In his message, Prakash said the incident had deeply affected his family, but thanked God that everyone was safe.

“Our biggest concern now is the safety and security of our family and loved ones,” he said.

Prakash said an incident of this nature was particularly frightening because it occurred inside their own home.

He urged members of the public to remain alert, look after their families and take steps to strengthen security around their homes.

He also stressed that the safety and wellbeing of his family remained more important than the material losses suffered during the robbery.

item.title: Fiji Rice board chair resigns
item.description: RAJ Sharma has resigned as the board chairman with Fiji Rice after holding the portfolio for several years. The resignation was confirmed by Minister for Public Enterprise Manoa Kamikamica during an interview in Labasa.
item.content:encoded:
RAJ Sharma has resigned as the board chairman with Fiji Rice after holding the portfolio for several years.

The resignation was confirmed by Minister for Public Enterprise Manoa Kamikamica during an interview in Labasa.

“I can confirm we have received a letter from Mr Sharma,” Mr Kamikamica said.

“He had suggested he wanted to focus on other portfolios.”

Mr Sharma’s resignation comes after several years of involvement with Fiji Rice, where he had been responsible for the portfolio and its related activities.

His departure is expected to bring changes to the management of the organisation as the relevant authorities consider the next steps.

The development comes at a time when the rice industry remains an important part of Fiji’s agricultural sector, particularly in the Northern Division.

Rice farmers have continued to face challenges including production costs, weather conditions and the need to improve local production.

Further details on Mr Sharma’s resignation and his successor will be announced by the relevant authorities.

Mr Sharma did not comment when approached for an interview.

item.title: Up to 5000 students drop out – Nabobo-Baba
item.description: UP TO 5000 Fiji National University(FNU) students were forced to drop out of their studies because they could not afford to pay their university fees. Professor Unaisi Nabobo-Baba said FNU is facing a $10million annual student debt crisis.
item.content:encoded:
UP TO 5000 Fiji National University(FNU) students were forced to drop out of their studies because they could not afford to pay their university fees.

Professor Unaisi Nabobo-Baba said FNU is facing a $10million annual student debt crisis.

Prof Nabobo-Baba said most of the outstanding debt was owed by private students.

“This is what was known in higher education as attrition,” she said.

She said the financial crisis affecting students went beyond unpaid fees, with about 10,000 students also going hungry because they could not afford basic food.

“When they are hungry, they can’t finish their studies and can’t come to school.”

She said students who struggled to afford food also faced difficulties meeting other essential costs, including transportation to and from classes. “If somebody is hungry, they can’t buy their basic food. They can’t catch the bus.”

She said the situation showed the need to support students not only to enter university but to complete their studies.

Prof Nabobo-Baba said the FNU Foundation was established through the support and generosity of individuals and organisations to help address the financial challenges faced by students.

“It helps address a gap in society and works towards creating a more equal playing field in education.”

She said education was a powerful tool for a developing country and students needed support to remain in education, complete their qualifications and succeed.

The Foundation, she said, was part of efforts to ensure financial hardship did not become a barrier for students seeking to build a better future through education.

item.title: inDepth I Beneath the numbers – ‘Property transaction volumes remain stagnant’
item.description: FIJI’S property market may look busy on paper, with more than 4000 properties changing hands in just 16 months. But beneath the numbers is a more sobering reality.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI’S property market may look busy on paper, with more than 4000 properties changing hands in just 16 months.

But beneath the numbers is a more sobering reality.

A study by South Pacific Property Consulting Services (SPPCS) Limited Managing Director Dr Abdul Hassan has found that property activity across Fiji remained relatively subdued between January 2025 and April 2026, with little evidence of sustained growth.

A total of 4037 properties changed ownership during the period, but Dr Hassan’s analysis shows that transaction volumes remained largely stagnant.

The figures raise a fundamental question for Fiji’s economy: if property is one of the clearest indicators of confidence, what does a stagnant market say about how confident Fijians and investors really are?

The report says the real estate sector is closely tied to the broader economy because property transactions reflect the confidence of households, businesses, investors and financial institutions.

“Property transactions reflect the confidence of households, businesses, investors, and financial institutions,” the report states.

And that confidence appears to be uneven.

Perhaps the biggest revelation from the study is where the property transactions are actually taking place.

Rural Fiji recorded 2224 property transactions, almost twice the 1169 transactions recorded in urban areas during the 16-month period.

The figures challenge the traditional perception that Fiji’s property market is primarily an urban story.

Instead, agricultural land, rural residential properties, undeveloped land and peri-urban development are driving a significant share of activity.

Nadi Rural was the standout performer, recording 462 transactions, representing about 20.8 per cent of all rural sales.

The report attributes this to continuing demand for residential subdivisions, tourism-related developments, agricultural land and investment opportunities along the expanding Nadi economic corridor.

Serua/Namosi followed with 253 transactions, Nausori Rural with 241 and Lautoka Rural with 228.

Together, those four areas accounted for more than half of all rural transactions.

The figures point to a property market increasingly stretching beyond traditional town boundaries as population growth, tourism and development push outward.

While rural Fiji dominated transaction numbers, Suva remained the undisputed leader among urban centres.

According to the report, Suva City recorded 330 transactions, accounting for about 28.3 per cent of all urban property sales.

Nasinu followed with 279 transactions, Lautoka with 191 and Nadi with 122.

The report says the stronger activity in these centres reflects population growth, employment opportunities and expanding commercial development.

But the picture changes dramatically outside Fiji’s main economic centres.

Labasa recorded just 28 urban transactions during the period.

Rakiraki had 13, Savusavu recorded eight, Tavua had three, Levuka recorded two and Sigatoka recorded just one urban property transaction.

It demonstrates that property investment remains heavily concentrated in places where jobs, infrastructure and commercial opportunities are strongest.

The numbers effectively reveal two different property markets operating within Fiji.

There is the concentrated urban market, driven by employment, population growth and commercial activity.

Then there is the rural and peri-urban market, where land, subdivisions, agriculture, tourism and future development opportunities are creating demand. According to the report, the Central Division accounted for approximately 38 per cent of all recorded property transactions, while the Western Division contributed about 36 per cent.

Combined, they accounted for nearly three-quarters of national sales.

The report says it reflects Fiji’s population distribution, stronger employment opportunities, infrastructure and concentration of commercial investment.

item.title: Shaw’s call for healthier lifestyles
item.description: FIJIANS should think about their health before they have a reason to worry about it. That is the message 21-year-old Kali Shaw hopes to take across the country as a contestant in the upcoming 70th Hibiscus Festival, where her advocacy is focused on raising awareness of non-communicable diseases and inspiring healthier lifestyles across Fiji.
item.content:encoded:
FIJIANS should think about their health before they have a reason to worry about it.

That is the message 21-year-old Kali Shaw hopes to take across the country as a contestant in the upcoming 70th Hibiscus Festival, where her advocacy is focused on raising awareness of non-communicable diseases and inspiring healthier lifestyles across Fiji.

“Genetics may load the gun, but it is our lifestyle that pulls the trigger,” she said.

Speaking during an interview in Suva, Ms Shaw said she grew attached to hospitals from a young age, an experience that helped shape her passion for medicine and her dream of becoming a doctor.

The Mokani, Tailevu native, who has maternal links to Kadavu, is the eldest of four siblings.

Ms Shaw said being the oldest has taught her responsibility and strengthened her desire to set an example for those around her.

She attended several primary and secondary schools before completing her high school education at St Joseph’s Secondary School.

While moving between schools was challenging, Ms Shaw said it taught her to adapt to different environments and understand different personalities.

Beyond medicine and advocacy, she has a strong interest in debating and reading, hobbies she said have helped shape her confidence and broaden her perspective.

“I also enjoy listening to ’70s music as a way of unwinding from the demands of medical school.” Her decision to enter the FMF Hibiscus Festival was further influenced by a healthcare outreach programme, where she observed people living with NCD-related conditions, including obesity.

item.title: Ratu Suliano backs needle exchange
item.description: TUI Namosi Ratu Suliano Matanitobua has backed the implementation of a needle and syringe exchange program as a measure to help reduce the spread of HIV, particularly among people who inject drugs. Speaking during a fundraising event for Navua Hospital, Tui Namosi described the proposed program as a positive step and said the issue would be raised at the upcoming Great Council of Chiefs (GCC) meet
item.content:encoded:
TUI Namosi Ratu Suliano Matanitobua has backed the implementation of a needle and syringe exchange program as a measure to help reduce the spread of HIV, particularly among people who inject drugs.

Speaking during a fundraising event for Navua Hospital, Tui Namosi described the proposed program as a positive step and said the issue would be raised at the upcoming Great Council of Chiefs (GCC) meeting.

He said the GCC would meet on August 17 and August 18, with the program among the matters expected to be discussed by members.

“After, we will make a paper and send it up to the main body.”

Health Minister Dr Atonio Lalabalavu has confirmed the program is in its final stages of implementation but stressed that public awareness and community acceptance would be critical before it begins.

“It has to be accepted by the community,” Dr Lalabalavu said.

“It must not be seen as a form of encouraging drug use.”

The program would provide sterile needles and syringes to people who inject drugs, reducing the risk of HIV transmission through the sharing or reuse of contaminated equipment.

Fiji recorded 2016 newly diagnosed HIV cases in 2025, a 27 per cent increase from the previous year, which has prompted renewed calls for harm-reduction measures such as a needle and syringe exchange program.

item.title: ‘Unsustainable’ – PM: Present economy cannot support $8 hourly minimum wage
item.description: PRIME Minister Sitiveni Rabuka believes an $8-an-hour minimum wage is not sustainable for Fiji at present. Mr Rabuka was responding to calls for the national minimum wage to be increased, including calls from the Fiji Trade Union Congress.
item.content:encoded:
PRIME Minister Sitiveni Rabuka believes an $8-an-hour minimum wage is not sustainable for Fiji at present.

Mr Rabuka was responding to calls for the national minimum wage to be increased, including calls from the Fiji Trade Union Congress.

Asked whether Government had plans to increase the minimum wage, he said there was a desire to do so but present economic circumstances made it difficult.

“There is a wish to do that. We are not able to do it,” the Prime Minister said.

He said any increase in wages had to be considered alongside productivity and the ability of businesses and the economy to support higher wages.

“So this thing involves everybody. So it’s got to be the productivity and the rewards.”

He said the call for an $8-an-hour minimum wage was unsustainable at the moment, “particularly with all the forces bearing on Fiji’s economy at the time”.

The issue of the minimum wage has been a subject of ongoing discussion between Government, employers and workers’ representatives.

Trade unions have argued that workers need higher wages to cope with the rising cost of living, while employers have raised concerns about the impact of higher labour costs on businesses.

He said Government recognised the desire for better wages but had to take into account the broader economic situation.

He added productivity would need to be considered alongside any future increases in wages.

item.title: Chiefly bure Vunisei
item.description: A research report documenting the traditional chiefly bure Vunisei was presented to the chiefly household of the late Tui Vuda, Ratu Eparama Tavaiqia, as part of an effort to preserve an important aspect of Fiji’s architectural and cultural heritage. The findings were presented on July 6 by University of Auckland researcher and Pacific architecture expert Dr Charmaine Ilaiu Talei, with support fro
item.content:encoded:
A research report documenting the traditional chiefly bure Vunisei was presented to the chiefly household of the late Tui Vuda, Ratu Eparama Tavaiqia, as part of an effort to preserve an important aspect of Fiji’s architectural and cultural heritage.

The findings were presented on July 6 by University of Auckland researcher and Pacific architecture expert Dr Charmaine Ilaiu Talei, with support from traditional leaders, local researchers, illustrators and Wayasewa builders from Namara Village.

Dr Talei said it was the first time Vunisei had been documented using architectural drawing methods and scientific knowledge.

“The report includes a building history of Vunisei, drone photographs of the site, architectural drawings and a number of high-quality photographs,” she said.

She said the research documented the building in detail, including its construction methods and architectural features, while using the Vuda dialect to identify and explain different architectural members.

“It’s very important for us that we present findings that are useful for our Fijian collaborators, something they can use to pass on to the next generation about maintaining and preserving the cultural knowledge of Vunisei,” Dr Talei said.

The report also includes photographs documenting the different types of magimagi used in the construction of the chiefly bure.

Dr Talei said the research team worked with Wayasewa builders to understand where building materials were sourced and how raw materials were transformed into materials suitable for construction.

She acknowledged the support of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fijian ecologist Dr Alivereti Naikatini, who assisted the research team with the scientific names of plants and the processes used to transform them into building materials.

“A lot of this knowledge is not common any more, and this is why this research was significant,” she said.

“Our buildings are endangered for many reasons, modernisation, climate change and natural disasters, so it’s important that we document this knowledge and have a good record of it so we can pass it on to the next generation.”

Dr Talei said the report would be available online as an open-access resource for people interested in learning more about the construction of the traditional chiefly bure Vunisei.

She said the open-access requirement also meant the research team had to carefully consider what cultural knowledge could be published.

“I have had to be very careful of the knowledge that the knowledge holders want to share.

“This is the reason, too, why we are presenting this report in case they want to pull back something and not include it because it will be open access, meaning you could just type in Vunisei and it will show up.”

She also thanked the Tui Sabeto, Ratu Viliame Mataitoga, for allowing the team to document the live construction of his chiefly bure, Erenavula.

Wayasewa builders were also involved in the construction of Erenavula, providing an opportunity for the team to further document traditional building knowledge and practices.

Taukei Nakelo Ratu Josaia Natakele, (green shirt) receives the report on the traditional chiefly bure Vunisei from Dr Charmaine Ilaiu Talei while Ratu Inoke Momoedonu looks on. Picture: SUPPLIED
